content: Vitamin C is generally a good source of nutrition, particularly in plant-based foods. However, the amount of vitamin C present in these foods depends on several factors, including the specific variety of the plant, the condition of the soil in which it was grown, the climate during its growth, the time elapsed since it was harvested, the storage conditions, and the method of preparation. The following data provides an approximate representation of the relative abundance of vitamin C in various raw plant sources. It is important to note that some plants were analyzed fresh, while others were dried, which can artificially increase the concentration of certain components like vitamin C. As a result, the data may vary and present challenges for direct comparison. The vitamin C content is expressed in milligrams per 100 grams of fruit or vegetable and represents a rounded average derived from multiple authoritative sources. Most animal and plant species synthesize their own vitamin C, making some, but not all, animal products a source of dietary vitamin C. Within animal tissues, vitamin C is most abundant in the liver and least abundant in muscle tissue. Since muscle tissue constitutes the majority of meat consumed in Western diets, animal products are not considered a reliable source of vitamin C. Vitamin C is present in human breast milk and, in lower amounts, in raw cow's milk. Pasteurized milk, however, contains only trace amounts of the vitamin. Any excess vitamin C in the body is excreted through the urinary system. Vitamin C undergoes chemical decomposition under certain conditions, many of which can occur during food preparation. Contrary to popular belief, boiling water at 100°C is not hot enough to cause significant destruction of vitamin C, as the nutrient only decomposes at 190°C. However, cooking methods such as pressure cooking, roasting, frying, and grilling are more likely to reach the decomposition temperature of vitamin C. Prolonged cooking times exacerbate this effect, as do copper cooking vessels, which catalyze the breakdown of the vitamin. Another way vitamin C is lost during cooking is through leaching, where the water-soluble vitamin dissolves into the cooking water, which is then discarded. However, not all vegetables lose vitamin C at the same rate; research indicates that broccoli retains more vitamin C than other vegetables. Additionally, studies have shown that fresh-cut fruit does not lose significant nutrients when stored in a refrigerator for a few days. Vitamin C is the most widely consumed dietary supplement and is available in various forms, including caplets, tablets, capsules, drink mix packets, multi-vitamin formulations, multi-antioxidant formulations, and crystalline powder. Time-release versions are also available, as are formulations containing bioflavonoids such as quercetin, hesperidin, and rutin. Tablet and capsule sizes range from 25 mg to 1500 mg. Vitamin C (as ascorbic acid) crystals are typically sold in bottles containing 300 g to 1 kg of powder, with one teaspoon of the crystals equating to 5,000 mg of vitamin C. Vitamin C is synthesized industrially from glucose via two main processes. The Reichstein process, developed in the 1930s, involves a single pre-fermentation step followed by a purely chemical route. The modern two-step fermentation process, originally developed in China in the 1960s, incorporates an additional fermentation step to replace part of the later chemical stages. Both processes yield approximately 60% vitamin C from the glucose feed. Research is ongoing at the Scottish Crop Research Institute to develop a strain of yeast capable of synthesizing vitamin C in a single fermentation step from galactose, a technology expected to significantly reduce manufacturing costs. Global production of synthesized vitamin C is currently estimated at approximately 110,000 tonnes annually. Major producers include BASF/Takeda, DSM, Merck, and the China Pharmaceutical Group Ltd. of the People's Republic of China. China is gradually becoming the dominant global supplier due to its ability to undercut the prices of U.S. and European manufacturers.
